chunks.text: Doc: MHD 17 (34660) WC August 2026 Scope This document provides information security controls, including implementation guidance, for health organizations. It is based on ISO/IEC 27002:2022 In addition to generic ICT equipment and software used in many other environments, the scope of this document includes software and systems specifically for healthcare, such as electronic health record systems and medical devices incorporating health software. Such medical devices can be programmed or programmable and can contain software, firmware or both. Other digital equipment (such as that for environmental and infection control, building management, and physical security), w hich can be used in premises where healthcare is provided, is also in scope. This document applies to information in all its aspects, whatever form the information takes (including text and numbers, sound recordings, drawings, images and video), by whatev er means it has been acquired or captured, whatever means are used to store it (such as printing or writing on paper or storage electronically), and whatever means are used to transfer or exchange it (orally, by hand, by post, movement of storage media, direct links or networking). This document is for organizations of all types and sizes that provide healthcare or are custodians of personal health information for other reasons. The information that they are responsible for can be stored and processed in many possible ways and locations, including on premises or in the cloud, but remains in scope. This document applies to all physical settings where healthcare is intended to be delivered, such as hospitals, clinics and other locations or facilities designa ted for healthcare purposes such as ambulances and mobile imaging or diagnostic units. It also applies to care provided elsewhere, such as in residential premises. In addition to the range of settings, this document applies to all methods of service provision including remote or virtual healthcare. The technical content of the document has not been enclosed as it is identical with the corresponding ISO standard. chunks.text: Doc: MHD 17 (34661) WC August 2026 Scope This document presents an informative set of common, high-level security-related capabilities and additional considerations to be used across the life cycle of health software and health IT systems, for the information exchange between the health software manufacturers (including medical device manufacturers ), healthcare delivery organizations (HDOs) and other stakeholders. It is applicable to health software running on any platform and in any environment such as cloud, on-premise or hybrid. Figure 1 provides a graphical representation of the health software which fully includes medical device software. chunks.text: FOREWORD Additive Manufacturing (AM), is a manufacturing process of joining materials to make parts from 3D model data, usually layer upon layer. In the field of medical devices, AM enables the fabrication of complex geometries, controlled porosity, lattice structures, internal channels, and patient-specific implants that are not readily achievable using conventional subtractive or formative manufacturing methods. For in vivo applications and implantable devices, the performance of additively manufactured products is influenced not only by the base material composition but also by feedstock characteristics, build orientation, layer thickness, energy input, thermal history, post-processing treatments, and surface finishing operations. The layer-wise fabrication mechanism can result in microstructural anisotropy, residual stresses, partially fused particles, internal porosity, and surface irregularities. These characteristics may significantly affect mechanical strength, fatigue resistance, corrosion behaviour, tribocorrosion performance, biological response, and long-term functional stability of implants. In addition, the digital workflow-from medical image acquisition (e.g., CT or MRI), segmentation, computer-aided design (CAD), data conversion (e.g., STL or AMF), slicing, and generation of machine-executable instructions- introduces specific considerations related to dimensional fidelity, geometric accuracy, coordinate integrity, and reproducibility. Errors in data processing or conversion may propagate through the manufacturing chain and influence final implant performance. Feedstock materials used in AM, including metallic powders, polymeric filaments, resins, gels, and composite biomaterial inks, require careful characterization with respect to particle size distribution, morphology, flowability, rheological behaviour, thermal transitions, crystallinity, chemical composition, and potential contamination. Material transformations during processing, such as oxidation, phase transformation, crosslinking, or degradation, can alter the physicochemical and mechanical properties of the final implant. Where multiple materials are combined, interfacial compatibility and interaction effects require additional evaluation. Post-processing operations such as stress relieving, annealing, hot isostatic pressing, UV curing, machining, abrasive finishing, chemical treatment, cleaning, and sterilization can substantially modify surface topography, microstructure, residual stress distribution, and material properties. These processes therefore require validation and verification to ensure that intended design characteristics and functional performance are achieved without introducing unintended defects or contaminants This standard provides technical guidance on: -feedstock material qualification and lifecycle considerations; -digital data acquisition, processing, and CAD-to-machine workflow; -design considerations specific to additive manufacturing, including lattice structures and minimum feature size; -process validation and control of AM systems; -post-processing, cleanliness, and sterilization considerations; -physico-chemical, mechanical, microstructural, and biological evaluation of AM implants; -test methods relevant to dimensional accuracy, porosity assessment, corrosion behaviour, tribocorrosion, mechanical performance, and structural integrity; -risk analysis aspects specific to additively manufactured

These include, but are not limited to: a) Vat photopolymerization, including Stereolithography (SLA) b) Powder bed fusion (PBF), including Selective laser sintering (SLS), Selective laser melting (SLM), Electron beam melting (EBM) c) Binder jetting d) Directed energy deposition (DED) Doc: MHD 20 (32899) WC MHD 20 (32899) WC Page 5 of 16

Differences may arise from: a) rapid solidification and cooling rates; b) layer-wise bonding mechanisms; c) residual stress development; d) partial fusion or entrapped feedstock; e) surface stair-stepping effects. These differences shall be considered during design verification and performance evaluation. 4.5 Biological and safety evaluation 4.5.1 Additively manufactured implants shall be evaluated for biological safety and performance in accordance with applicable standards. 4.5.2 Biological evaluation shall be conducted using a risk management approach in accordance with , taking in to consideration: IS 17932 a) the nature of body contact; b) the duration of exposure; c) the material composition and potential process-related changes; d) residual materials arising from additive manufacturing and post-processing; e) degradation products, where applicable. 4.5.3 Where process-specific characteristics such as porosity, lattice architecture, residual feedstock, or surface modifications may influence biological response, additional evaluations shall be performed as appropriate. 5 FEEDSTOCK MATERIALS 5.1 General 5.1.1 Feedstock materials used for additive manufacturing of implants shall be selected and qualified to ensure that the final manufactured product meets specified mechanical, physicochemical, and biological requirements. 5.1.2 Feedstock shall be considered a critical input material whose properties directly influence the microstructure, crystallinity, porosity, surface morphology, and functional performance of the finished implant. chunks.text: 6.1 The design of additively manufactured implants shall ensure that the finished device meets specified functional, mechanical, physicochemical, and biological performance requirements. Design shall consider: a) intended clinical application; b) anatomical constraints; c) loading conditions; d) material properties; e) additive manufacturing process limitations; f) post-processing requirements; g) process-induced anisotropy; h) dimensional variability inherent to additive manufacturing. 6.2 Design activities should take into account: a) The opportunities and design freedoms that AM offers designers b) The issues that designers should consider when designing parts for AM c) Warnings to designers, or red flag issues, that indicate situations that often lead to problems in many AM systems. 6.3 Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM) 6.3.1 Design shall account for process-specific capabilities and limitations, including: a) minimum feature size relative to machine resolution; b) overhang limitations; c) support structure requirements and removability; d) achievable surface finish; e) thermal distortion and shrinkage; f) build orientation effects; g) layer bonding characteristics. 6.3.2 The resolution of the additive manufacturing system shall be considered to avoid mismatch between design intent and machine capability, which may result in unintended geometric artefacts or porosity. 6.3.3 Design modifications introduced to ensure manufacturability shall be verified for performance impact. 6.4 Design Controls 6.4.1 Computer-Aided Design (CAD) Models a. Designs for additive manufacturing shall follow the principles of functional integration, minimum feature size, and support structure minimization. b. These may include cleaning to remove residual debris, controlled cooling (also called annealing), and/or additional steps such as drilling, cutting, polishing, and sterilization. 7.2.3 Process Validation and Verification: Some device or component characteristics can be checked individually after they are produced to make sure they will function properly and meet specifications. This is especially true of geometric features which can be checked quickly and nondestructively. When other functional features, such as mechanical strength, cannot be checked individually because the test could destroy the object or is impractical, manufacturers validate their processes prior to production. Process validation ensures that a manufacturing process will produce product that is within defined specifications, as long as specified processing parameters are monitored and controlled. 7.2.4 Testing: Device testing methods and results are submitted to the FDA to show that the device meets regulatory requirements and is reasonably safe and effective for its intended use. Each device or type of device has its own set of tests that may be based on FDA Guidance documents, international standards, or internal process controls. Devices manufactured by 3D printing are generally subject to the same regulatory requirements as more traditionally manufactured medical devices. 7.2.5 Requirements for post-processing for powder bed fusion. Mechanical testing of implants manufactured using AM can have additional requirements for sample preparations, considerations for test setup and reporting requirements. It is important to understand gaps between requirements in existing implant standards and possible additional requirements for AM specific sample preparation, testing and reporting. If multiple different materials are used during the additive manufacturing process, like support materials in material jetting or in multimaterial implants, the interaction of these materials can have a significant influence on the properties of the manufactured implant. b) Material properties - It is important to be aware that changes to the material properties can occur at all stages of the AM process and post-processing from feedstock to final output. For instance, oxygen intake or cross-contamination between different materials (e. g. in multimaterial builds) can occur during the AM process and affect the material properties (e. g. the physical and/or chemical properties). c) Lattice structure - Lattice structure can for example be assessed with stereological evaluation, compression testing, X-ray diffraction and shear fatigue testing. It is important to be aware that complex features such as lattice structures can lead to unstable features at the boundary of the material. d) Support structure - Some implant geometries might need structures to provide a base and anchor for the part during the AM process to manufacture the part as intended and ensure the intended properties of the finished implant. Supports are typically removed from the part prior to use. Considering the extent of removal as well as the method used for removal of the support structure can be critical during the risk analysis, since remaining support structures can for example affect the functionality of the finished implant. e) Material-related post-processing - Common post-processing procedures to reach the intended material properties are thermal treatment, UV-light post-exposure or treatment with solutions of defined pH or salinity. IS 19491 The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test shall be conducted by immersing the test sample (working electrode) together with a KP-113 saturated calomel reference electrode and a PtP-201 platinum auxiliary electrode into 250 mL of Ringer’s solution (NaCl 8.6 g/L, KCl 0.3 g/L, CaCl ₂ ·6H ₂ O 0.48 g/L) maintained at 37 ± 1 °C and pH 7 ± 0.2. The sample shall be stabilized for 120 minutes to determine its open-circuit potential (Eocp), after which EIS measurements shall be carried out using an AutoLab PGSTAT 302N system equipped with an FRA2 module. The impedance spectra shall be recorded in the frequency range of 10 ⁴ Hz to 10 ⁻ ³ Hz with a sinusoidal voltage amplitude of 10 mV. The resulting data shall be fitted to an equivalent electrical circuit using the least squares method to calculate impedance, resistance, and capacitance values, and the results shall be presented as Nyquist and Bode plots for interpretation of surface layer properties. 9.3.5 Scratch test The adhesion of layers to the titanium alloy substrates shall be evaluated using a scratch test performed with a Rockwell diamond cone indenter under gradually increasing normal load. The test shall be conducted in the loading force range of Fc = 0.03–30 N, with a loading rate of vs = 10 N/min, a table speed of vt = 10 mm/min, and a total scratch length of l = 3 mm. The critical load (Lc), representing the minimum normal force that causes loss of adhesion between the coating and the substrate, shall be determined based on recorded changes in acoustic emission, friction force, and friction coefficient, as well as by microscopic observation of the scratch track. 9.3.6 Microgap Analysis The microgap inherently occurring or formed during the process of 3D printing may affect the mechanical stability and characteristic. Hence the porosity of the dispensed material in the Definitive Parameter Print Output shall be analysed and documented. IS 1586 9.4.5 Post-processing of Additively Manufactured Products Additively manufactured products shall undergo post-processing, where applicable, to ensure conformity with specified requirements relating to mechanical properties, dimensional accuracy, surface characteristics, corrosion resistance, and biological performance. Post-processing procedures shall be defined, validated, and controlled. The manufacturer shall establish documented acceptance criteria based on the intended use of the implant, material specification, design features (including porous or lattice structures), and applicable regulatory requirements. Post-processing may include one or more of the following, as appropriate: a) Mechanical processes, such as machining, grinding, polishing, or abrasive blasting, to achieve specified dimensional tolerances and surface finish requirements. These processes shall not introduce surface damage, microcracks, or contamination. Functional porous or osseointegrative regions shall not be adversely altered unless specified by design. b) Thermal processes, such as stress relieving, annealing, or hot isostatic pressing (HIP), to modify microstructure, reduce residual stresses, or improve mechanical performance. Time–temperature–pressure parameters shall be controlled and recorded. Where applicable, mechanical properties and microstructural characteristics shall be verified following treatment. c) Chemical or electrochemical processes, such as etching, passivation, electropolishing, or coating, to improve surface finish, corrosion resistance, or biological response. Process parameters shall be controlled to prevent harmful residues. Coatings, where applied, shall meet specified requirements for thickness, adhesion, and uniformity. Following post-processing, implants shall be cleaned using validated procedures to remove residual powders, process media, and contaminants. Cleanliness shall be verified by appropriate inspection or testing methods. Verification shall demonstrate that post-processing achieves the intended functional outcomes without adversely affecting implant safety or performance. Records of post-processing parameters, inspection results, and validation data shall be maintained to ensure traceability. 9.5 The geometric capabilities such as accuracy, resolution etc. of the AM system shall be tested. 9.6 Star artefacts containing predefined geometric features may be used as reference specimens to assess the capability of non-destructive testing methods in detecting additive manufacturing defects such as porosity, lack of fusion, dimensional inaccuracies, and internal discontinuities. chunks.text: Doc: MHD-08 (34193) WC April 2026 4 All dimensions in millimetres Fig.3 Scaler, Dental , No. SC 5/6 5 REQUIREMENTS The requirements specified in Clause 4 of IS 3887 shall apply. 6 WORKMANSHIP AND FINISH The requirements specified in Clause 7 of IS 3887 shall apply. 7 HEAT TREATMENT The scalers except the carbide tip shall be uniformly hardened and tempered to a hardness of 430 to 490 HV , when tested in accordance with IS 1501(Part 1). 8 TESTS 8.1 Practical Test The working end of the instrument shall be applied to the top of a compression type spring balance at an angle of 20° approximately. A force of 3 kgf (30N approximately) shall be applied for 30 seconds while gripping the handle at about the middle of its length. On releasing the force ,the instrument shank shall not show any sign of damage or acquire a permanent set. 8.2 Elasticity Test The handle of the instrument shall be gripped in a vice so that the whole length of the shank protrudes out of vice jaw. A force of 3 kgf (30 N approximately) shall be applied at a distance of 2 mm from the end in a direction at right angles to the plane o f the working end. On releasing the force, the instrument shall not show any sign of damage or acquire a permanent set. The test shall be repeated on the other end also.

chunks.text: Doc No: MHD-08 (34260) WC May 2026 2 1 SCOPE This standard prescribes the requirements and the methods of sampl ing and test for autopolymerizing (acrylic) resin for dental use. 2 REFERENCES The standards given below contain provisions which, through reference in this text, constitute provisions of this standard. At the time of publication, the editions indicated were valid. All standards are subject to revision, and parties to agreements based on this standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the most recent editions of these standards. IS No Title IS 4905 : 2015 ISO 24153 : 2009 Random Sampling and Randomization Procedures (First Revision) 3 REQUIREMENTS 3.1 Description The material shall be supplied in the form of powder and liquid. 3.1.1 The powder shall consist essentially of polymerized esters of acrylic acid, substituted acrylic acid or interpolymers of these with each other or with vinyl esters. 3.1.2 Liquid – The liquid shall consist essentially of monomeric material appropriate to t he powder. It shall be clear and no substantial colouration shall be produced when it is exposed in a clear glass container to bright diffuse daylight for 24 hours. It shall be free from deposits or sediments and, when maintained at a temperature of 60 ± 2 °C for 24 hours in a closed vessel in the dark, it shall not show evidence of thickening. 3.2 The powder and liquid shall effect a satisfactory repair, when used in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions, which shall not produce local tissue reaction or general toxic effects. 3.3 Hardening – The resin shall be capable of being ground and polished to a high gloss within 30 minutes from the commencement of mixing, when processed in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. 3.4 Colour – The colour shall be as specified by the purchaser. When coloured resin shall be translucent and evenly coloured and when clear, resin shall be clear and colour less. 3.5 Crazing – When prepared as prescribed in A -2, specimen plates shall show no appreciable evidence of crazing when viewed with the naked eye. 3.6 Surface Properties – When prepared as prescribed in A -2, the material shall have a glossy surface. 3.7 Freedom from Porosity – When prepared and sectioned as prescribed in A -3, the material shall not show excessive bubbles or voids on visual examination with a magnification of 5 x when sectioned.

chunks.text: Doc No: MHD-08 (34260) WC May 2026 4 A P P E N D I X A (Clauses 3.5 to 3.11) METHODS OF TEST FOR AUTOPOLYMERIZING (ACRYLIC) RESINS FOR DENTAL USE A- l. TEST CONDITIONS A-l.1 All tests shall be carried out in a room in which ambient conditions are as follows: Temperature 27 ± 2˚C, and Relative humidity 55 to 75 percent. A-2. TEST FOR CRAZING AND SURFACE PROPERTIES A-2.1 Apparatus –_A denture flask complying with the dimensions shown in Fig. 1, filled with gypsum except for a space in which a tapered rectangular specimen plate of the following dimensions can be processed: Upper surface 65 x 40 mm Lower surface 64 x 39 mm Thickness 5 mm A-2.2 Procedure A-2.2.1 Line the space in the denture flask throughout with tin-foil, and prepare clear resin of the hot-processing type, without cross-linking agents, pack into the space provided and process in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Prepare two such specimen plates. A-2.2.2 Saw each plate crosswise in halves and round and polish the sawn edges. Store the halves of each plate in water at a temperature of 37±1°C for not less than 7 days. Whilst still immersed. Then bring to room temperature immediately prior to repairing, wipe the halves of each plate dry and place in their original relative positions in the flask but allowing a gap of 3.0 ± 2 mm between the prepared edges. Join the halves immediately using the repair resin in accordance with the Manufacturer’s instructions. A-2.2.3 Upon removal from the flask, examine the specimen plates for compliance with the requirement for crazing properties and the repair material for compliance with the requirement for crazing and surface properties.

Examine repair material for compliance with the requirement for freedom from porosity. A-3.2 Prepare six repair specimens each measuring 64 (± 2) x 10.00 (± 0.03) x 2.50 (± 0.03) mm from these strips for other tests in the following manner, A-3.2.1 Mill evenly the strips on both moulded surfaces and the edges so that the dimensions are slightly oversize. The load exerted by the deflection measuring device over its entire operating range shall be acc ounted for when calibrating the machine load. A-4.1.2 Bending Rig –– The loading nose and the two supports shall have highly polished cylindrical surfaces 3.2 mm in diameter and parallel to within 0.1 mm over a 10 mm length. The distance between the centres of the supports shall be 50 ± 0.025 mm. The loading nose shall be midway between the support to within 0.025 mm. Means shall be provided to prevent misalignment of the specimen on the supports. A-4.1.3 Water-Bath –– A bath capable of maintaining the specimen at a temperature of 37.0 ± 1.0°C. A-4.2 Procedure A-4.2.1 Subject each of the six specimens prepared in A-3.2 to the following test: Place the 10 mm side of the specimen symmetrically on the supports and allow the immersed specimen to come into equilibrium with the water-bath temperature of 37.0 ± l.0˚ C. Apply an initial load of 1.5 kgf to the specimen and measure its deflection. It s hall then be continuously loaded at 18 ± 3 mm/min to break. Record the deflection to the nearest 0.5 mm at a load of 2.5 kgf and again at a load of 4.0 kgf. A-4.3 Result –– Report the average deflections at the centres of the six specimens tested to the nearest 0.05 mm

chunks.text: Doc: MHD-08 (34260) WC Aug 2026 7 A-5.1 Preparation of Test Specimens –– Prepare the resin and pack into a stainless steel mould of the dimensions shown in Fig. 2 mounted in gypsum in the two halves of a denture Bask. Process according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The disc so prepared shall be 50 ± 1 mm diameter and 0.5 + 0.1 mm thick. The surface of the disc so prepared shall be smooth and the top and bottom flat. A-5.2 Apparatus –– Two desiccators containing silica gel freshly dried at a temperature of 130°C. A-5.3 Procedure A-5.3.1 Bring one of the desiccators to a temperature within the range of 35 to 39°C and the other to a temperature within the range of 20 to 25°C. Prepare a disc of resin (see A- 5.1) and place in the desiccator maintained at a temperature within the range 35 to 39°C. Then transfer for one hour to desiccator maintained at a temperature within the range of 20 to 25°C. At the end of this period, weigh to the nearest 0.02 mg. Repeat this cycle until the loss in mass of the disc is not more than 0.4 mg. Record the mass of the disc. A-5.3.2 Immerse the disc for 24 hours in distilled water maintained at a temperature within the range 35 to 39°C. At the end of this period, remove the disc from the water with tweezers, wipe with a clean dry hand-towel until free from visible moisture, wave in the air for 15 seconds, and determine its mass within 1 minute after removal from water. A-5.3.3 Place the disc for 24 hours in the desiccator maintained at a temperature within the range of 35 to 39°C. At the end of this period, transfer it to the desiccator maintained at a temperature within the range 20 to 25°C. At the end of this period, weigh to the nearest 0.2 mg. Repeat the drying till the loss in mass of the disc is not more than 0.4 mg. Record the mass of the disc. Test two such specimens. Retain the specimens after the test for use in the determination of colour stability (see A-6). A-5.4 Result A-5.4.1 Water Absorption - Record the difference between the first and second mass and report the average of the two results as the water absorption of the material. DETERMINATION OF COLOUR STABILITY A-6.1 Apparatus A-6.1.1 Lamp - A lamp fitted with an oxidized aluminium reflector (see Fig. 3) 360 mm in diameter at the lower rim and a light source known as an S -l bulb which has been in use for not less than 50 nor more than 400 hours. This light source rated at 400 watts is a combination tungsten-filament mercury-arc enclosed in glass which filters out ultra-violet light below 28 000 nm (2 800 A). A-6.1.2 Turntable - A turntable which can be operated at 33 rev/ min. The turntable shall support an aluminium disc fitted with a suitable specimen holder such that the distance from the Centre of the specimen to the center of the supporting disc is 12.5 cm. A-6.2 Procedure - Place one of the discs used for the determination of water absorption and loss in mass by leaching (see A-5) in the holder and centre the aluminium disc under the S-l bulb so that the plane of the specimen is 18 cm below the bottom of the bulb. Revolve the turntable and disc at 33 rev/min and expose the specimen to the radiation of the lamp for 24 hours, after which period compare it with the unexposed specimen by visual inspection in bright diffuse daylight. Record the colour of the specimen as stable if no more than a slight change in colour, perceptible with difficulty, is apparent.

WORKING RANGE TEST A-l.1 Apparatus A-1.1.1 Water-Bath A-l.2 Procedure - Adjust and maintain the water -bath at the desired working temperature range (see 4.7). Take 30 ± 2 g of the material, place in the water -bath and warm for 15 minutes. Remove the warmed material from the water-bath and work (knead) in wet hand for 15 seconds. Return the material to water -bath and condition for an additional 5 minutes. Remove the material from the water -bath again and work (knead j in wet hand until the material loses plasticity or proper working consistency and can no longer be moulded by finger pressure. The total time elapsed from final removal from the water-bath to the loss of plasticity shall be termed as working time. A-2 FLOW TEST A-2.1 Apparatus, A-2.1.1 Flow Testing Machine- The flow testing machine (see Fig. 1) consists of a weight A, a non -conducting shaft B and a brass platen C. The total weight in air of the three components is 2 kg. The weight A shall be separated from the platen C on the shaft B by a minimum distance of 75 mm. The shaft shall be hard rubber or a similar poor thermal conductor to avoid loss of heat due to conduction. The diameter of the brass platen which touches the test specimen shall be not less than 50 mm. The thickness of the platen shall not exceed 6.5 mm.
